translations.text: Yesterday’s discourse about the body amazed us. It explained the beauty of nature and marveled at the wisdom of its architect.
For when nature is explained, the Creator is glorified; and when the work is praised, it brings honor to the craftsman.
But while we were occupied with this, the time for the evening service arrived. While the lamp of the body was being proclaimed, the evening lamp was brought forward for the service of the church.
And to that same lamp was added the mention of a third lamp, that of the divine laws.
The first lamp, that of the body, has the testimony of the Giver of Life himself: “The lamp of the body is the eye.” And the lamp made from fire is known to everyone through experience and habit.
And the third lamp is proclaimed by David: “Your words,” he says, “are a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.”
But today the teaching of our honored father, the father of us all, showed us yet another lamp, that of the Gospel.
A lamp that does not rise in opposition to the sun, but obeys the Sun of Righteousness.
Christ comes to be baptized, and John baptizes him, not puffed up with arrogant pride, but serving the divine command.
A man who himself needed baptism baptized the Baptizer and Lord of all—not approaching presumptuously, but obeying the command.
John is a lamp who bears in himself the pattern of the saints of the Old Testament. Just as the Jews called the Law a lamp, so those who practiced virtue according to the Law were also called lamps.
Pay attention, I beg you. John is a lamp, because the Law and the Prophets lasted until John. David is a lamp, because when, in his old age, he boldly sought to go to war against Zabron,
the elders of the people restrained him and would not let him go to battle. They all raised their voices in protest: “Do not go to battle, lest you extinguish the lamp of Israel.”
David is a lamp; John is a lamp. But since the true Light, the Sun of Righteousness, dawned and sent out his brilliantly shining and clear rays from heaven,
those who practice virtue through that light surpass [?] the lamps. Those others shared the name of the lamp because they had served according to the Law, which was called a lamp.
But these, enlightened by the light of the Gospel, who live according to it and display that same manner of life, have passed beyond the rank of a lamp and are called light.
Although a lamp is also light, what comparison can it have with light itself? And whatever the order of nature gave, the King’s generosity bestowed upon his disciples.
And see Christ’s love for humanity: he made his disciples share in the name he gave himself. “I am,” he says, “the light of the world.”
And elsewhere: “You are the light of the world.” Oh, these new graces and gifts, which surpass all words and thoughts!
See how his love for humanity overcomes the order of nature. He makes the sun rise. And why do I say that he makes the sun rise?
Rather, when he sends out its forerunner, the dawn in the east, he puts all the hosts of stars to flight, and all the stars hide and conceal themselves.
Not that they perish, but they are concealed by the greater light of the sun.
But Jesus, the Sun of Righteousness, who dawned after the former night, not only illuminated those prophets
who shone at his coming, like stars, but also gathered other lights to himself.
Lights dawned together with the Sun of Righteousness: heralds of truth, those who marshal the ranks of worship of God.
Of these Paul says, “Among them you will shine as lights in the world, holding fast to the word of life, so that I may boast on the day of Christ.”
Have you seen the rays of the Sun of Righteousness? Look also at the evangelist: how he gives names that stand above all the names used in rhetoric,
above all those of vain philosophy, above those of grammarians and practitioners of the arts, and indeed above all titles of honor and distinction—the names of sons.
What does this mean? Rustic names and heavenly minds accomplish great deeds.
Bartholomew and Thaddeus are names foreign to the Greek language, yet they cast aside all [?] and plant the whole of knowledge in its place.
The Life-giver chose fishermen, not to reject the wise or to discredit the eloquent, but to keep the beginning of the preaching free from suspicion.
The word is preached through fishermen so that the power of the one who accomplishes the work may become evident.
We marvel not because they are fishermen, but because through fishermen the power that is above the world was proclaimed.
God could have stirred eloquent men to champion the preaching, so that the wisdom of the knowledge of God might be revealed.
But he did not wish to make the truth of the cross ineffective. Therefore Paul also said, “I did not come with superiority of speech, so that the cross of Christ might not be made ineffective.”
That is, so that it might not be considered something futile and rejected through arguments. Rather, the power of the crucified one planted the Church through the company of the apostles.
He planted the word of truth through untrained tongues, which had been instructed only in the divine law. And after planting it through them, he then watered it through the wise as well.
He did this not without purpose, lest those who devise excuses for sins should say, “He deceived the ignorant, but could not bring the wise and powerful to assent.”
Rather, against those whose minds were inclined toward deception, he skillfully employed fishermen, the foolish, the ignorant, and the incapable.
For this reason, although not among them, God raised up articulate and eloquent preachers already in the time of the apostles.
“A certain Alexandrian named Apollos,” it says, “a Jew by birth, came to Ephesus, eloquent and powerful in the Scriptures and in thought, and articulate in interpretation.”
“Powerful,” it says, “in the Scriptures.” And what skill did he possess? He was a great help to those who had believed.
“In the public squares,” it says, “he refuted the Jews.” Do you see the sword of Christ, how it is sharpened in everyone?
He trains the fishermen and arms the wise. And because eloquence serves error, he often strips evil of its weapons and equips virtue with them.
Error is clothed in reasoned arguments; truth seizes them and destroys error with those very arguments.
Likewise, when the blessed David brought down the giant Goliath, he first wounded him with his own weapons and then cut off his head with that foreigner's sword.
Taking it from him, he beheaded him with it. In the same way, truth knows how to draw the sword of error and destroy error itself with it.
There were wise men among the Gentiles; Christ sent zealous men from among the Jews to contend with them.
Among the Jewish people there was a sword of steel: Saul, who had gone astray in opposition to the churches and was cutting and [?] the faith of Christ.
The Life-giver took that same sword and placed it in the Church's hands, to drive away every evil that might rise against it.
And this is precisely what blessed David said: “The sinners drew their swords and bent their bows. Their swords will enter their own hearts, and their bows will be broken.”
God spoke through the wise, and he also spoke through the ignorant, so that through both he might display his power:
through hunters, so that with untrained tongues he might reject the artfulness of useless words; and through the wise, so that with deep understanding he might expose deep cunning;
and, building a wall around the faith, he might strengthen humankind. And what he did among the ignorant and the eloquent, he also did among kings. Listen to how this happened.

At the beginning of the preaching, the Life-giver could have brought kings into obedience to the preaching at the very first opportunity and raised them up as fellow combatants for the worship of God, as they are now.
But he did not do so, lest he cast doubt upon the truth, as though the church had been established through human protection and not through the power of God.
He stripped it of human assistance and clothed it with heavenly power.
Until the deeply devout Constantine, thirty-five kings ruled over the Romans, one after another, and they were unwilling to submit in obedience to the faith,
so that I might teach that grace receives no human power from a vessel, but has its own power by nature.
And because he saw the whole world in error, lest those who make excuses for their sins should again say, “He was able to deceive the ignorant and the unsuspecting,
but was unable to bring kings and rulers into his grasp,” he kindles the message, brings kings under the yoke of the worship of God, and leads all [?] into a single unity in the truth,
so that it might be evident that the King of kings and Lord of lords displayed the surpassing greatness of heavenly wisdom through humble preaching.
Today the names of the apostles are read aloud; the fishermen were proclaimed; the words of the unlearned resounded, and they bestowed every instruction upon the world.
And pay attention to [?]. “The first of the twelve,” it says, “was Simon, who was called Peter,” the rock of the church, the foundation of the worship of God.
He had the name Simon from his father and mother, but he was named Peter by the Life-giver. “You are Peter,” he says—which means “rock”—“and upon that rock I will build my church.”
All the preaching of the church stands established upon rock, and all heretical error upon unstable clay.
The firm rock, which supports the building above it, is one thing; the unstable soil, which gives builders no firm footing, is another. It is not even stable in itself.
Their words are unstable, their speech is cold, and their beliefs are deserving of reproach, because human ideas have also been mixed into the faith of God.
And the clay strives to shake the rock, but the rock does not succumb to defeat. “The gates of hell,” he says, “will not overpower it.”

The disciples of heretics are like clay workers who mold bricks, for they temper the [?] of the clay with some straw, and in this way make what is loose harder, so that what is crumbling appears solid.
It appears solid as long as nothing harmful has come upon it. But if rain, a flood, fire, or anything else strikes it, it does not stand firm.
For this reason, the prophet speaks to those who put their trust in earthly things and suppose that nothing bad will come from them,
saying: “Thus says the Lord: Go down into the clay, tread it with straw, and make yourself harder than brick, and fire will consume you.”
He rebukes those who put their trust in bodily and earthly things and suppose that any power is free from defeat.
The foundation of the church is the rock, and that of the heretics is Jerusalem.
The prophet wished to show—or rather, God himself through the prophet—what sort of church it is that is established upon the rock, and what sort of Jewish fold this is,
which does not remain firm and stable. He says to the prophet Ezekiel, “Take a brick for me, mark Jerusalem on it, and surround it with a siege wall.”
Why a brick? So that you may learn the characteristics of the brick and of the rock. Jerusalem stood upon a brick, but the foundation of the church is the rock.
Indeed, even if we call the church a rock, we do not lie. Nor do I deny the rock upon which it stands. The church too is a rock, because it has Christ as its firm rock,
and another rock, Peter, who received his name through his confession: “You are,” he says, “the Christ, the Son of the living God.”
But I [?] to clarify this: why did John the evangelist, who was so full of excellence that he gathered the showers of the gospel into himself—
the son of thunder, who drew into himself the whole abundance of grace at once—not adopt Peter’s expression at the beginning of his Gospel? He did not say, “In the beginning was the Son,”

nor, “In the beginning was the Only-begotten.” Instead, leaving aside the titles “Son” and “Only-begotten,” he turned to “Word”: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

Peter was called blessed not because he called him the Word, but because he confessed him as the Son. Why, then, did blessed John leave aside the expression that brought this blessing and turn to “Word”?
The apostles knew what they were preaching, but those who were to receive it from them could not bear the loftiness of their words.
For at the beginning of the preaching, the word sounded in ears both worthy and unworthy. So that they would not taint divine teaching with human thoughts,
and, on hearing “Son,” imagine a father and mother, bodily substance, and the other needs of the flesh,
he therefore turns to the designation “Word,” which could explain the absence of passion at the very beginning of his utterance.

And see what an order he employs: he sets up a ladder and leads us through many distinctions to the summit, the designation “Son.” He did not deny that designation, but reserved it for the appropriate time.
“In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word,” so that you may learn the absence of passion and the freedom proper to his begetting. For the mind is the constant father of the word.

“In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word.” Nor would it even be called a word on its own if it were not someone’s word. And whose Word would it be? “In the beginning,” he says, “it was with God, and the Word was God.”
First he explains the passionless begetting, and then he shows the inseparability of his personal existence with the Father, the unity of their nature, their wills, and their activity.
“And the Word was God.” By this he doubles the honor, he says. And what lies before us is that what is needed is not [?] words, but assurance of the realities.
“In the beginning was the Word” makes known the passionless begetting. “And the Word was God” makes known the inseparable unity.
“And the Word was God” makes known the uncorrupted honor. “He was in the beginning with God.” He repeats it to establish the same meaning.

And because he called him the Word, while the word as it exists among us does not clearly reveal the likeness of what is being discussed, he sets out his statement more clearly and shows him to be at once God, Word, and Creator: “And all things came into being through him.”
And in this the heretics find certain remedies. “He said ‘through him,’” they say, “not ‘from him’ or ‘out of him,’ but ‘through him.’”
But I wanted to learn with certainty from those who stumble, who do not know their own nature and fall into such stumbling blocks,
and who subject that nature which surpasses every mind to investigation and examination.
What difference do they suppose there is between “through him” and “from him”? For we must not pronounce judgment at random, but show confirmation from the Holy Scriptures.

What does “through him” mean? “The Father created through him,” they say. They take refuge behind that particular expression as a fence, and use it as a shelter for their evils, bringing forward the statement, “The Father created through him.”
Tell me the manner of it, and do not merely bring forward the expression in a confused jumble. I cannot understand an expression empty of meaning, for I am ignorant.
As for “through him” in things done among us, it is possible to understand the circumstances: a master works through a servant.
One gives a command, and the other carries out the command. A master works through a craftsman: one sets out the pattern, and the other fashions the work.

Now tell me the manner of it: how would he work through the Son? Would he give a command as a master does to a servant, or would he go to a skilled worker as someone without skill, or would he, like a craftsman,
fashion the work with an adze or a saw or some other tool? Whatever manner you mean, make clear what you understand, so that I may learn what I believe.

Did he command as a master commands a servant, or did he, as someone without skill, give the work to a craftsman, or did he, as a craftsman, work with a tool? Come, tell me what manner you suppose it was.

“As a father through a son,” he says. You have not yet made clear what I want, for I am not asking about the persons of the speaker or the hearer, or the form of the one giving the command and the manner of the one receiving it.
“The Father commanded, and the Son worked,” they say. Show the manner of the Son’s creating and the Father’s commanding. “The Father gave a command by speech, and the Son worked,” they say.
In what manner? Did he work by putting his hand to the task? That signifies undergoing bodily toil, if he performed some operation.
“No,” they say, “rather, he himself created by speech.” See how their wickedness multiplies! Tell me the utterance the Father spoke; set before me the word by which the Son created.
But so that I may not allow you to [?] and say whatever you wish, I will [?] you, willingly or unwillingly, into divine teaching, and show you the Creator’s utterances.
God said, “Let there be light.” God said, “Let there be a firmament.” Who was it who spoke? Immediately they counter, “The Father spoke, and the Son carried out the command.”
If these were words of someone giving a command, God would not have said, “Let there be light,” but “Make the light”; and the Son would have heard and made it.
But please tell me: why is the same utterance found in both cases: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light,” and again, “God said, ‘Let there be a firmament,’ and there was a firmament”?

If the Father used that utterance, “Let there be light” and “Let there be a firmament,” why did that same utterance not act and accomplish the work, but instead require another utterance? This is a weighty matter.
Write that the Father spoke, as the heretics say, and the Son stood nearby and heard what God said, “Let there be light,” and that the Son received the utterance and made the light.
Could those frenzied minds be so audacious as to say that the Word of God underwent bodily activity and toil?
And if they persist in claiming some bodily activity rather than divine power, David comes forward and rebukes them: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established.”

Now if the Father said, “Let there be light,” and the utterance that went forth accomplished no work, but waited for the Son, was the Father lacking something, and did he make up his deficiency through the Son?

He said, “Let there be light,” and nature did not accompany it. He said, “Let there be a firmament,” and the word accomplished no work. Rather, the Father spoke and waited for the Son’s creative work.
See what you are doing! Perhaps, while devising this argument, you introduce another impiety, as though the Father were weak and the Son powerful.
Come, speak! Explain what “through the Son” means. “Through the Son,” they say, “he made the creatures.” Who made him? The Father made him.
May Christ forgive these terrible sins, for I shudder even at the words when I hear this account of blasphemy.

And do not be surprised at this. For when he was about to introduce the heretics’ blasphemy, he did not introduce it in explicit words, but took care. He did not state the blasphemy openly, but under a disguise.
Thus, even when he spoke to God himself, he said, “Come now, touch his flesh, and see whether he will not bless you to your face,” instead of saying, “May you be cursed.”
The disciples of the heretics say this—let it be heard as coming from them, not from us: “The Father,” they say, “made only the Son, and the Son made all the other creatures.”

Explain how he came into being. If the Son came into being by God’s will, we too came into being by God’s will, as did the other creatures. What distinction will there be between those who worship and the one who receives their worship?
If he came into being in the same way as I did, why should he demand worship from me?
If he came into being from nothing by God’s will, and the world came into being from nothing by God’s will, I do not see what distinction there will be between them.
If God the Father [?] him in between, and the Son the other creatures—if there is any distinction between them by which the Son came into being, say so.

But if there is none, and the Son came into being from nothing solely by God’s will, and all the other creatures came into being from nothing by his will, how can one who came into being from nothing by God’s will, just as we did, receive worship from us?

“Yes,” they say, “he receives it, because he is not like the other creatures. He surpasses every creature; he surpasses every order of things that have come into being.” They devise clever arguments with mere words, and dishonor his nature.
It is not because he is above the creatures that he ought to receive worship from creatures, unless he is the Creator and Lord of the creatures, and [?] from nonexistence.
For a creature does not receive worship from creatures. The heavens are greater than the earth, but the earth does not owe worship to the heavens.
The stars are greater than plants, but plants do not bow down to the stars. An angel is greater than a human being, but a human being does not bow down to an angel.
And why should I even speak of human nature? How is an ant like Gabriel, or a gnat like Michael?

Yet because those are creatures and these too are creatures, where worship is concerned the angels descend to their level, and these lowly creatures rise to theirs, and they are crowned in worship around the throne.
By their superiority, those are distinguished and separated from these; but in being creatures and in worship, they are united and close to one another.
And listen to the blessed David: “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” he says, “praise him in the heights. Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his hosts.”
“Sun and moon, all stars and light, and the heaven of heavens, and the waters that are above the heavens.”
And when he has finished listing those that are above the world, he adds to the same passage, “Praise the Lord from the earth.”
With the same utterance he prescribes the same worship: angels do not bow down in one way and human beings in another.
“Praise the Lord from the heavens,” he says, “praise the Lord from the earth. Praise him, all his angels, dragons and all the depths.” How can angels be like dragons?
Fire and hail, snow and frost, wind and storm, wild beasts and all livestock: bears, lion, leopard, panther, boar, and all wild beasts; livestock: camel, donkey, ox.
All these worship together with them, not because they take into account superiority of rank, but because they recognize the honor shared by all in worship.
“Wild beasts,” he says, “and all livestock, creeping things and birds.” Ravens praise together with angels. “Creeping things,” he says: vipers, snakes, scorpions, and every kind of creeping thing.
Do you see that superiority in honor does not diminish the worship offered by those of lower rank?
For it is not that, because those are more exalted creatures, these should have no share in worship, but that the Lord’s honor and divine being should be glorified by all.
For all creatures owe worship to the Creator. But now show the difference that lies between them.
When you say of the Father that everything is from him, you show his superiority by your expression alone, without a word.
For heretics blaspheme with their faces even before their words. When they argue about the Father, they begin to say, “One God, the Father, from whom are all things,
and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.” Before your tongue speaks, your face blasphemes; before your words, your expression belittles him.
Oh, the ingratitude! The prophets magnify even the creatures, while the heretics belittle the Creator.
David honors and exalts the creatures: “How great are your works, Lord!” The godly magnify even the works, while the ungodly belittle even the Creator.
“They magnify the creatures,” they say, “because they do not have greatness of themselves. But one must not magnify the Son beyond what he is, raising his honor to a certain degree.”
As though they had the authority to pity the Son and show him kindness! They speak impiously; they act impiously, not understanding the meaning of their words.
But I know that Christ is magnified, not by any addition to his nature, but by the gratitude of those who worship him.
Listen to blessed David as he magnifies him: “I will praise the name of my God with praise,” he says, “and magnify him with thanksgiving.”
It is not that he makes him great from being small; rather, he magnifies the benefactor who was thought small by unbelievers. “I will make him great with thanksgiving.”
Paul magnifies the giver of life: “Whether by life or by death, Christ will be magnified in my body.” Why does he magnify him? Because he cannot find the measure of his greatness.
Why does he magnify him? Because he cannot attain that honor with a human tongue. He magnifies not the nature of those being glorified, but the words of praise.
I magnify Christ as much as I am able, not because I can speak in proportion to his greatness.
Just as the godly magnify God, so too they exalt him.
“I will exalt you, my God and my King.” Do they perhaps bring him from a low position to a high one?
What, then, does “I will exalt” mean? It stands for saying, “I will proclaim your exaltation.”
And since human nature is not sufficient, [?] the divine Scriptures give the command: “Exalt the Lord our God.”
For he is even beyond exaltation, and his exaltation [?] is measured by your glorification.
Therefore the three wise young men, who made the furnace a church and turned the flame into dew by the power of faith, praised as far as they could and left what was beyond their ability [?].
“Bless the Lord,” they say, “all you works of the Lord; bless him and exalt him still higher forever.”
They did not consider it enough to exalt him, but sought to exalt him still higher, for they saw human weakness exposed by his surpassing greatness.
Here, too, the three young men, acting with care, bring all created things to worship.
For they mentioned the angels, the archangels, the powers, the waters, the sun, the moon, the rivers, the springs, the earth, and its fruits;
the sea and [?], the birds and the livestock, the wild animals and the creeping creatures, and human beings.
Among all these they introduced no mention of the Son, nor any mention of the Holy Spirit, for the Son does not belong among those who worship, but among those who receive worship.
But perhaps someone will say, “How could the three young men bring the Son to worship when they did not even know that he was the Son?”
They were not aware of this, for the prophets did not speak openly and plainly about the Son’s honor.
But the name of the Holy Spirit was proclaimed through them. Although the Son’s name seemed unfamiliar to them, that of the Spirit was openly evident.
As Isaiah also says, “They rebelled and angered the Holy Spirit”; and the blessed David says, “Do not cast me away from your presence, Lord, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me.”
See how firm the argument is: David and Isaiah did not come after the three young men, so that no one may say, “At that time it was not known, but afterward it was revealed.”
The three young men came after David and Isaiah, and therefore they were familiar with the writings of the prophets and knew that the Holy Spirit had been proclaimed.

Why, then, do they bring all those created things to worship and not mention the Spirit? They mention the angels, the archangels, the powers, and the others one by one, yet they do not mention the Spirit.
For they saw him not joined with created things, but revealed as [?]. For they too had been enlightened by the Holy Spirit,
and, strengthened by the power of the Holy Spirit, they trampled the fire, like iron [?], or something refined into steel and tempered, becoming still harder and sharper.
Likewise, when the souls of the righteous are tempered by the Holy Spirit, they regard fire as nothing, and also water, heaven, earth, and everything in them.

But so that I may [?] these words, and so that the disciples of the heretics may not needlessly regard them as conjectures, I will [?] the argument from Paul, who lists the Savior’s works of creation.
The heretics willfully [?] this, turning the statement “It came into being through him” upside down to show by it some inferiority in the Son.
Elsewhere Paul does not say “through him,” but “by him himself.” “By him,” he says, “everything was established, whatever is in heaven and whatever is on earth.”

Pay close attention: “Whatever is in heaven and whatever is on earth.” So that he may not lead us into conjectures and needless stumbling, he lists the created things, to preserve the uncreated nature undefiled.
“Everything,” he says, “came into being through him, whether thrones, dominions, or authorities”; and again, “By him everything was established.”
What is “everything”? Thrones, authorities, dominions, principalities: everything was established through him and in him.
And not only through him and in him, but by him and in him. He is before everything, and everything was established by him.
And why did he leave out those created things as well, and not mention the sun and moon, heaven, earth, the stars, or everything else?
For it is quite clear that visible things belong to the order of created things; therefore he leaves out what is obvious. And because among invisible things there are ranks of worshippers,
and the uncreated nature that receives their worship, he considers it necessary to enumerate everything that is above the heavens,
so that he may keep the Holy Spirit free from blasphemy and give the heretics no cause to rejoice.
“Everything,” he says, “came into being through him: whether thrones, principalities, powers, or dominions.” And he did not mention the Holy Spirit.

Now let them say how the heretics arrived at that conclusion, for they did not hesitate, through our weakness, to pour out blasphemy and fill every city with it, as though the Church preached three almighty beings.
But I would like to persuade them once again not to blame us, but the prophets.
If I were putting forward words from my own thoughts and devising innovations against the truth, then they would rightly accuse me.
But if we repeat the words of the prophets, the accusation falls not on us who explain them, but on those who established the teachings.
We have spoken not as they blasphemously alleged, but as we believe. The Church acknowledges not three almighty beings, but one power that holds everything.
Almighty power is truly recognized in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
Let anyone who speaks of three gods separate from one another be accursed; and let anyone who does not confess the Trinity as one Almighty be accursed.
But do not consider these words strange or new when you see blasphemy poured out against the truth; call to mind [?] the earlier saints.
Stephen saw the heavens opened and the Savior at the right hand of God. He proclaimed what he saw, and because of his proclamation he was suspected of blasphemy.
When that holy, resounding trumpet sounded, saying, “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God,”
the Jews could not endure the truth, but stopped their ears, as though blasphemy were being spoken and not the truth proclaimed.
And now do not consider it anything new or strange if a truthful statement is regarded as blasphemy, for wickedness habitually attributes its own faults to virtue.

If we have embellished anything, we shall be judged for that embellishment. If we have devised any innovation, we shall give an account for devising it. But if the words of the prophets are being recounted, what fault is ours?
Thus says the Lord Almighty: “Behold, I will come and dwell in your midst,” says the Lord, “and many nations will take refuge in you, and you will know that the Lord Almighty sent me.”
Why do you find fault with our words and not with those of the prophets? They boldly pronounce judgment in truth. Where there is truth, there is no fear at all.
Where there is faith, apprehension does not arise. Where there is faith, there is strength; and where there is unbelief, there is apprehension.
The giver of life said to the disciples, “Why are you fainthearted and without faith?” Do you see? Where there is unbelief, there is faintheartedness; and where there is faith, there is strength.
“Stephen,” it says, “full of faith and power, performed great signs among the people.” And Paul says of Abraham that he did not waver in unbelief, but grew strong in faith.
I too dare to say that the name of the Father is also that of the Son. “Blessed,” it says, “is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” And the giver of life says, “I have come in my Father’s name.”
Let us ask what the Father’s name is. The Scriptures proclaim “God” and “Lord” as the Father’s name: “This is my name.”

Pay close attention. “I am,” he says, “the Lord God; this is my name.” If “Lord” and “God” are names of the Father, and I find the same names belonging to the Son, is it not clear that the Son is Lord and God?
“Blessed,” he says, “is he who is to come in the name of the Lord. The Lord our God has appeared to us. Blessed is he who has come in the name of the Lord.”
Therefore blessed Thomas, seeing that the name belonging to the Father also belongs to the Son, and having received actual proof of the resurrection, cries out loudly, “My Lord and my God!”
Let us see whether God has any other name in which the Son does not share. “Let them know,” he says, “that your name is Lord.”
But when I say “shares,” I do not mean anything bestowed by grace, but a sharing by nature.

David says, “Let them know that your name is Lord, and you alone are exalted over all the earth.” And the apostle says, “For us there is one Lord, Jesus Christ.” “One” and “alone” have the same force.
The schismatic assigns the name “God” to the Father and “Lord” to the Son. Since you have assigned “Lord” to the Son, and the prophet says, “Let them know that your name is Lord,
and you alone are exalted over all the earth,” will you dare to say that there is one Lord, and that Jesus alone is exalted, and not the Father?
Pay attention. How will you dare to say that Jesus is the one Lord when you hear the prophet say, “Your name is Lord, and you alone are exalted”?
If you understand this as referring only to the Father, can you deny that Jesus is Lord? And if, in turn, you understand it as referring to the Son, can you conclude that the Father is not Lord?
Far be it! Rather, let those words of yours agree with your thoughts, and do not call him Lord in words while considering him a servant in your thoughts.
“Do you call the Father Lord?” “Yes,” he says. “Do you also call the Son Lord?” “Yes,” he says.
And how do you say there that he alone is Lord and exalted, and here that there is one Lord? Hence you must not count, but believe.
If I call the Father God, the Son God, and the Holy Spirit God, you call me a believer in three gods.
And if he calls the Father Lord and the Son Lord, what shall we call him? A believer in two lords, perhaps?
Pay attention. You dare to speak of two lords: even if not in words, you nevertheless think of them that way.
For you say that the Father's lordship is one thing and the Son's lordship another: the one has unrestricted authority, while the other is subject to the Father's lordship.
If that is so, there is no longer one Lord, nor does their lordship have one dignity and nature. The two cannot be called one Lord if the Father is one kind of Lord and the Son another kind of Lord.
I wonder how you can serve a divided lordship, when the Lord himself says, “You cannot serve two masters.”
But let us proceed to what lies ahead. The Father is Lord and God; the Son is Lord and God, as has indeed been shown: “Let them know that your name is Lord,” and “There is one Lord,
Jesus Christ.” Let us see whether we can find any other name of God in the Scriptures.
Blessed Moses says, “If the children of Israel ask me, ‘What is the name of the one who sent you?’ what shall I say?”
See here too the blessed one who is to come in the name of the Lord. Pay attention to how he gives the true identifying signs: “You shall say, ‘He Who Is has sent me.’”
If that is so, the Father's name is “He Who Is.” Let us see whether the Son also has the same name; otherwise our defense is in vain. “He Who Is,” he says, “has sent me.”
What do you say to the apostle? “By ‘He Who Is,’ whom am I to understand—the Father or the Son?” You are full of great folly in asking, “The Father or the Son?”
You divide the honor and do not recognize their equality in honor. Whom would you call “He who is”? The one whom the Scriptures named, whom I myself proclaimed.
Moses calls the Father “He who is,” and I call the Son “He who is”: “I have sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart for my brothers and my kinsmen according to the flesh,
who are Israelites, to whom belong adoption, the giving of the law, worship, the covenants, and the promises;
to whom belong the fathers, and from whom came Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever.”
Do you see how the name of the Father and the name of the Son agree with one another in words and in reality? “He who is sent me.” “He who is over all, [?], blessed forever.”
Is the statement somehow forced, and does it not bear witness by the facts themselves [?]? Why do you condemn our language and disdain the words of the prophets?

Let us consider another name as well. For it was not without reason that it was said, “Blessed is he who is to come in the name of the Lord.” Rather, every name belonging to the Father belongs also to the Son.
The blessed Isaiah says to the people, “You have forsaken the Lord God your Savior, and have not remembered the Lord your helper. Therefore you will plant an unfaithful plant and unfaithful seed.”
“For you have forsaken God your Savior.” God’s name is Savior; God’s name is Helper. Now let us see whether the Son too is Savior.
Listen to the angels who praised and brought good news to the shepherds. “We bring you good news,” they say, “of great joy, for today a Savior has been born to you, who is Christ the Lord.”
“You have forsaken,” he says, “God your Savior, and have not remembered the Lord your helper.” And where will you find the Son called Helper?
A man [?], it says, and God [?] to him his demon-possessed son. He says, “Good teacher, I brought my son to your disciples, and I could not heal him.”

And the Savior says, “How long has it been?” Not so that he himself might learn, but so that those standing nearby might learn how long the affliction had lasted that he was clearing away, and might benefit.
“Since childhood,” he says. “It often throws him into fire and into water. I spoke to your disciples, and they could not heal him. But if anything is possible, help us.”
Pay careful attention. He accepted the man’s approach, but rejected his approaching with a doubting mind.
If someone says to God, “If anything is possible,” that does not befit God. Rather, the other statement does: “Everything is possible.”
And because he approached him as a prophet or an apostle who possessed some limited power, who could do some things and could not do others,
the Savior then mocks his foolishness—or rather, corrects his ignorant mind—because he said, “If you can.” And by his silence [?] he rebukes his impudence.
“Everything,” he says, “is possible for the one who believes.” He does not make anything plain in words, but the man standing nearby understood his anger from his face.
When he saw that the giver of life was reproaching him and showing his anger in his face, what plea did the man who had sinned cry out? “I believe,” he says, “Lord; help my unbelief.”
This was instead of saying, “I have sinned; I did not know your power. Make up what I lack; help my unbelief.” For it was unbelief to say, “If you can, help.”
But the father of the demon-possessed boy repented, while the misguided heretics do not repent, though they often call upon the Son in their prayers.
Oh, the folly! You may write that you do not regard the Son as equal in honor to God, nor the Spirit of the Son; will you not regard him as equal in honor to the prophets?
Have you not heard the words of the prophet Elijah? “If I am a man of God,” he says, “let fire come down and consume you, the captain of fifty, and your fifty men.”

The prophet commands with full authority, and is the Lord of the prophets to offer prayers? Elijah commands creation with authority, although he was not its lord, because he had boldness through his devotion to God.
There one could see a man of flesh giving orders to flashing fire and bringing fire down upon his opponents.

Elsewhere the same blessed Elijah says to his disciple, “Ask something of me before I am taken up from you, and I will do it for you.” He did not say, “I will intercede,” but, “I will do it before I am taken away.”
The prophets command with full authority through the power of their faith, yet do you call the Lord of the prophets into submission and consider yourself a participant in his prayers?

Does not even Joshua, the Lord’s namesake, put you to shame? He stopped the sun without prayers. Did he say to the Lord, “Stop the sun”? Rather, he said with full authority, “Let the sun stand still.”
The servant became so powerful—or rather, the Lord’s very name did. It was not that anything stood in awe of him, but of the royal name.
And will Truth itself not perform acts of kindness with full authority, but instead become an intercessor? But let us turn to the matter before us.
The Father’s name is “He Who Is,” and the Son’s name is “He Who Is.” The Father’s name is “Helper,” and the Son’s name is “Helper.”
The Father’s name is “Almighty,” and the Son’s name is “Almighty.” If I say this by issuing a ruling of my own, do not accept it. But if I demonstrate it, do not dispute it.
See what you will [?] if you dispute what I say. You insult the prophets; you deny God if you insult the prophets, and, advancing still further, you will fall into impiety.
If you regard the words spoken by the prophets as something of my own, you insult not me, their interpreter, but the utterances of the prophets and the inspiration of God.
Do you not know that God considers insults against the prophets to be against himself? When Samuel was rejected by the people, what did God say?
“It is not you they have rejected,” God says, “[?] me.” And to make it clear that whoever does not listen to a teacher and prophet does not listen to [?], he says to Ezekiel:

“Son of man, go to the rebellious house and speak with them. They will not listen to you, because they do not wish to listen to me. If they listen to you, then they also listen to me; and if to me, then also to you.”

It has already been shown that the Son is called Almighty. But another prophet also bears witness: “He who builds his ascent in heaven and establishes his good news upon the earth—the Lord Almighty is his name.”
And who is it who built his ascent in heaven and established his good news upon the earth, if not the one who said to his disciples as he ascended, “I am with you until the end of the world”?
“Behold, I will come,” says the Lord Almighty, “and I will dwell in your midst.” What does “I will dwell” mean?
The evangelist explains: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” “Many nations will take refuge in the Lord, and you will know that the Lord Almighty sent me.”
“Where,” they say, “is it written that the Son is Almighty?” Where is it written that the Father is Almighty?
You demand words; I demand words. You gather strength; I muster strength. Speak from the prophets; receive from the prophets.
“Search the Scriptures,” says the Savior. No one searches for something that is evident, but for what is hidden. “Search,” he says, “the Scriptures.”
See how the Trinity is proclaimed in forms of a single authority. Listen to [?], who says, “Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who lead the people astray.”
Pay close attention: “Those who bite the heralds with their teeth speak peace with their mouths, yet peace was not given into their mouths.”
So that no one should listen to the false prophets. But I, he says, will be filled; I will be filled with power by the Spirit of the Lord.
Either accept this and believe, or erase it from your mind, for you cannot erase the living Scriptures.

So that no one, he says, should listen to false prophets. But I will be filled with power by the Spirit of the Lord. He cannot say, “With my own spirit,” but rather, “I will be filled with power by the Spirit of the Lord.”
Who says this? Explain the words to me, so that I may understand the meaning of the power.
And in another place God says, “I will no longer continue to have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will stand against them in opposition.
But I will have mercy on the children of Judah, and I will save them through the Lord their God.” And will you not save through yourself, but through another God?
The schismatics do not understand that the words of the prophets are veiled. If he proclaimed them openly, that would not be prophecy, but proclamation.
It would not be prophecy, but gospel. Whatever is manifest is gospel, and whatever is wrapped up is prophecy.
“And you, Daniel,” he says, “seal the words of this vision,” instead of saying, “Cover them in obscurity.”
He does not mean, “Hide the writings,” which people read to this day, but the meaning of the words. The words of the prophets were sealed, and they are explained through the gospel.
Again God says to the people, “What shall I do with you? You have not accepted correction.
I slaughtered your prophets with the sword of my mouth, yet even so you did not listen to me. I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.”
And why do you not say, “As I overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah,” but instead, “As God overthrew them”? Did you perhaps liken yourself to another?
“I overthrew you,” he says, “as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. Yet even so you do not believe me.”
Do you see the power concealed? Rather, he has illuminated it plainly and openly. Do you see the power of devotion to God speaking boldly?
And now, why should you find fault with someone who calls the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit almighty?
Just as, when I say, “God and God and God,” I do not mean three gods, but one,
so, when I say, “Almighty and almighty and almighty,” I do not mean three almighty beings, but one.
Let the Savior’s words put you to shame. He said to the Jews, “It is written in your law that the testimony of two people is trustworthy.” When he says, “God and God,” do you not believe?
Yet even when he says, “I and the Father,” he does not mean two gods separate from one another, but the one divinity of himself and the Father.
And he makes this clear in another saying: “I and my Father are one.” He says “one” because of their inseparability, and “we are” so that no one may regard the persons as lacking personal existence.
Let us spare our souls and [?]. Spit out that poison, wipe away the rust, scrape away the copper, and submit to God, to whom even the demons submitted.

Let changes in circumstances put you to shame. Do not believe in church and become a heretic when you go outside. Do not show reverence for the word here and, when you go outside, stray into brutishness.
A fickle soul does not remain settled amid changes and does not become steadfast. A God-fearing soul passes through changes, but does not itself change.

The person devoted to God remains devoted to God even in war, struggles steadfastly in famine, and does not grow slack in abundance. The person devoted to God is self-controlled and enduring in everything.
does not change with the changes of nature. The spirit of a righteous person is neither shaken by the turmoil of wars nor made lazy by the abundance of comforts.
When right glorification is proclaimed, he is found to be an eager listener; and toward the obstinate, he is eagerly obstinate. He does not separate himself from unity and has no divided mind.
There is one Lord God. Come, let us follow him. But if you follow error, you will arrive at error.
Just as fine wine is not harmed by changes—even if you transfer it from vessel to vessel, its taste and character remain the same—bad wine is quickly exposed by such changes.
Likewise, the spirit of a God-fearing person is not overcome by changes but overcomes change. A more shallow spirit, however, is quickly exposed.
These are not my words, but those of the blessed prophet Jeremiah, who cried out against the nation of the Moabites.
For they had enjoyed ease for a time and thought that they would enjoy ease [?], and they mocked Jerusalem’s captivity.
The prophet rebukes them: “Do not boast of your ease, and do not grow proud of the success of your affairs, for you have not yet experienced change. Your change too will come.”
He has not yet taken action to test their intentions. And what does he say? “Moab has been at rest from his youth and has experienced no change through adverse [?] circumstances.”
“Moab has been at rest from his youth and has grown proud in his glory. He has never been poured from vessel to vessel.”
This is another way of saying, “He has never gone into captivity.” Therefore his taste remains in him, and his smell remains unchanged.
Brothers, we must also bring forward the example of divine teaching sealed in the holy Scriptures.
What likeness is there in speaking of divinity in terms of wine? Yet the prophet’s teaching is unfailing salvation.
“Moab,” he says, “has been at rest from his youth and has grown proud in his glory. He has not been poured from vessel to vessel and has never gone into captivity.”
“Therefore his taste remains in him, and his smell remains unchanged.” The Church was tested by evil and poured from vessel to vessel,
from peace into war and from war into peace, and its sweet fragrance remained. “We are a sweet fragrance,” he says, “in Christ.”
I have spoken about all this, and I know that I have made my speech long. But since I have been slandered, I had to show that I was in the right.
For such slander has spread throughout all the churches: if someone has spoken badly, everyone is nevertheless under reproach.
I have made a defense on behalf of myself and the whole Church: the Church has one Lord, one God, one Creator, one Almighty, and one King.
But when you hear “one,” understand God as the inseparable Trinity, the endless and incorruptible kingdom, glory and truth. It is never divided, but exists and remains eternal and life-giving.
May all of us enjoy him in truth and give glory to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
